summary: An IP over InfiniBand link-layer address is 20 octets, larger than the 16 octets reserved for the hardware address in DHCP and BOOTP messages. This document describes how to use the DHCP message fields when running DHCP over IPoIB. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: The address space on a form is too short for InfiniBand's long names. This explains how to fill out the form anyway.

questions: why is chaddr too small for ipoib
subtitle: How DHCP clients on InfiniBand fill in message fields when the link address is too long for the hardware address slot.

tldr.problem: An IP over InfiniBand link-layer address is 20 octets, but the DHCP and BOOTP "chaddr" field is only 16 octets, so a DHCP server cannot learn the client's link address or unicast a reply to it.
tldr.mechanism: The client sets htype to 32, hlen to 0, zeroes chaddr, always sends a client-identifier option, and sets the BROADCAST flag so the server broadcasts its reply.
tldr.outcome: DHCP works over IPoIB without changing the DHCP message format. This is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 4390 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Address That Does Not Fit
sections.content:
DHCP (RFC 2131) hands out IP addresses and settings to hosts. It is built on BOOTP, and the client's hardware address travels in the chaddr field of the message. When a client has no IP address yet, the server uses that hardware address to unicast its reply.

The chaddr field is 16 octets long. The IP over InfiniBand (IPoIB) link-layer address is 20 octets long (RFC 4391). It simply does not fit, so the server cannot unicast a reply to the client. This RFC clarifies how the DHCP fields are used over IPoIB so that implementations interoperate.
sections.eli5: The box on the form is 16 letters wide but the InfiniBand name is 20 letters long. So the server cannot read the name and cannot send a private reply.

sections.title: The Workaround in Outline
sections.content:
Because the server never receives the link-layer address, a DHCP client MUST ask the server to send a broadcast reply by setting the BROADCAST flag whenever IPoIB ARP is not possible, that is, when the client does not know its IP address.

The RFC admits that RFC 1542 discourages broadcast replies, but says that for IPoIB this is a necessity. To keep broadcasts from piling up at subnet startup, it points to the advice in RFC 2131 that a client wait a random time of 1 to 10 seconds before server discovery. The same delay spreads out the servers' broadcast responses.
sections.eli5: Since the server cannot find the client's mailbox, it announces the answer to everybody and the right client picks it up. Waiting a random moment first stops everyone from shouting at once.

sections.title: Field Values for IPoIB Clients
sections.content:
A DHCP client on an IPoIB interface MUST follow these rules:

  • htype (hardware address type) MUST be 32.
  • hlen (hardware address length) MUST be 0.
  • chaddr (client hardware address) MUST be zeroed.
  • The client-identifier option MUST be used in DHCP messages, and it MUST conform to RFC 4361.

Normally chaddr is unique in the subnet and identifies the client interface. With it zeroed, another unique value is needed, which is the job of the client identifier option.
sections.eli5: The client leaves the too-small box empty and writes its unique name on a separate line instead, so the server still knows who is asking.

sections.title: The BROADCAST Flag and Later States
sections.content:
A DHCP client on IPoIB MUST set the BROADCAST flag in DHCPDISCOVER and DHCPREQUEST messages, and set ciaddr to zero. This makes the server, or the relay agent, broadcast its reply.

Once the client has an address the rules change. Per RFC 2131, ciaddr MUST be filled in with the client's IP address in the BOUND, RENEWING or REBINDING states, so the BROADCAST flag MUST NOT be set. The server then unicasts the DHCPACK to the address in ciaddr, and the link address is resolved by ARP.
sections.eli5: While the client has no address, it asks for shouted answers. After it has an address, people can send answers straight to it, so no shouting is needed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to RFC 2131 for the security considerations relevant to DHCP and states that this document does not introduce any new issues.

The author acknowledges that the document borrows extensively from RFC 2855, DHCP for IEEE 1394.
sections.eli5: This change only fills in a form differently, so it adds no new dangers beyond the ones DHCP already has.
